input.question: How is it that your veins/arteries don't simply cut off whenever you sit or compress the body in normal circumstances?
input.ground_truth: For the most part veins and arteries are not on the surface so simply sitting won't compress them enough to "cut off" flow, but it can be significant enough to reduce flow to the point your leg "goes to sleep" , also why you should not have legs crossed when taking your blood pressure, etc. Also the circulatory system is remarkably complex and closing one pathway often is compensated for by blood rerouting through alternate, less restricted, paths.

Okay, let's imagine your body is like a house with lots of little tubes inside. Some tubes bring food and stuff to different rooms (that's like your blood bringing things to your body), and some tubes take the trash away (that's like blood taking things away).

Now, if you sit down or squish your body, it might look like those tubes could get squished shut, right? But your body is really smart! The tubes (veins and arteries) are strong and stretchy, kind of like soft, bendy straws. They can move and bend when you sit or move, so they don’t get closed up.

Also, your body has little valves in the veins, like tiny doors that help the blood keep moving the right way, even if you’re upside down or sitting. And your heart is like a pump that keeps pushing the blood along, so it doesn’t stop flowing just because you sit down.

So, even if you sit or squeeze your body a little, your tubes don’t get cut off because they’re strong, bendy, and your heart keeps them moving!
